### What is the Book of Jeremiah about?

The Book of Jeremiah gives the prophesies of a priest named Jeremiah. It also tells how Jeremiah suffered in different ways while he prophesied.

Jeremiah began prophesying about 626 B.C. After the death of King Josiah, many groups of people in Israel opposed Jeremiah. Some of these people wanted to depend on Egypt to protect the nation. Others were idol worshipers. They hated Jeremiah for denouncing their gods. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/falsegod]])

During the reign of King Jehoiakim, Jeremiah prophesied about the temple of Yahweh. King Jehoiakim received some of these prophecies in writing and burned the document. The next king, Zedekiah, put Jeremiah in prison when he told the king to surrender to Babylon.

King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylonia invaded Judah in 597 B.C. He conquered Jerusalem in 587 B.C. He offered Jeremiah housing and money if Jeremiah would go to Babylon. But Jeremiah remained in Jerusalem to help the few Jews left there.

Shortly after that, Gedaliah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had chosen to be governor over Judah, was murdered. Some Jewish rebels captured Jeremiah and took him to Egypt. Those rebels went to Egypt to be protected there rather than to live under Nebuchadnezzar’s rule. Jeremiah may have died soon after being taken to Egypt. But while in Egypt he prophesied that the Babylonians would invade and conquer Egypt.

### How should the title of this book be translated?

The traditional title of this book is “The Book of Jeremiah” or just “Jeremiah.” Translators may also call it the “The Book about Jeremiah” or “What the Prophet Jeremiah Said.” (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-names]])

### Who wrote the Book of Jeremiah?

Jeremiah was a priest and a prophet living in Judah. He spoke the prophesies in the Book of Jeremiah. A friend named Baruch wrote down many of the prophecies as Jeremiah spoke them to him.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

### What is the new covenant that is presented in the Book of Jeremiah?

Jeremiah introduced a “new covenant” between Yahweh and Israel (chapter 31). Yahweh would “write this covenant on the hearts” of the people. This means that the covenant would be a part of the people instead of just written on stone or paper. The people would obey the new covenant with all their heart. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenant]])

### What relationship do Jeremiah’s prophecies have to the other nations besides Israel?

Much of the Old Testament before this time is only about the nation of Israel. But Jeremiah also spoke of how Yahweh would judge other nations of the world. Yahweh would also punish the other nations for their wicked deeds. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/judge]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]])

## Part 3: Important Translation Issues

### Are the events in the Book of Jeremiah told in the order that they actually happened?

Many of the events in the Book of Jeremiah are not told in the order that they actually happened. Instead, the various prophecies appear to be arranged by topic.

### Why does the Book of Jeremiah refer to this prophet as “he” or “him”?

Many times in the book, the author refers to Jeremiah as “Jeremiah” or “he.” This is unusual if Jeremiah wrote the book. The reason this occurs is perhaps because Baruch, Jeremiah’s secretary, wrote down some parts of the book. Translators should keep the words “Jeremiah” and “he.”

# Jeremiah 1 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

The chapter moves from a dated heading (1:1–3) to Jeremiah’s call (1:4–10), two visions (1:11–16), and Yahweh’s charge (1:17–19). The ULT formats 1:5 and 1:7–8 as poetry.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Commissioning a prophet

Yahweh set Jeremiah apart before birth and put his words in Jeremiah’s mouth. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]])

# Jeremiah 2 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This is a covenant lawsuit in poetry. Yahweh recalls Israel’s early devotion (2:1–3), indicts the nation for abandoning him (2:4–19), and exposes its unfaithfulness (2:20–37).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Israel as an unfaithful wife

Yahweh pictures the covenant as a marriage, so idolatry appears as prostitution. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/prostitute]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Rhetorical questions

Yahweh accuses mainly through rhetorical questions, and paired lines often restate one idea.

Jeremiah is using **the word of Yahweh was to me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh gave me a message.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh spoke a message to me, saying]

Jeremiah is using the words translated as **And the word of Yahweh was to me** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

Quote: הָלֹ֡ךְ וְ⁠קָֽרָאתָ֩ בְ⁠אָזְנֵ֨י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֜ם לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Go and proclaim in the ears of Jerusalem that I, Yahweh, say this]

# Jeremiah 3 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Poetry and prose alternate: there is an appeal to unfaithful Judah (3:1–5), a contrast of apostate Israel and treacherous Judah (3:6–11), a call to return (3:12–18), and a closing confession (3:19–25).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The law about divorce

Verse 1 assumes the existence of the law forbidding a remarried woman to return to her first husband (see [Deuteronomy 24:1-4](../deu/24/01.md)). Yahweh applies it to Israel and Judah as adulterous wives. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/adultery]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

Yahweh, the prophet, and the people all speak, and the changes are unmarked.
The term **Saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

# Jeremiah 4 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter moves from a call for Israel to return to Yahweh (4:1–4) to poetic alarm over an invading army from the north (4:5–31).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Circumcision of the heart

In [4:4](../04/04.md), circumcision, the covenant sign, is an image of inward devotion. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/circumcise]])

# Jeremiah 5 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is mostly poetry about a search through Jerusalem for one just person (5:1–9), a warning of an invading nation (5:10–19), and an indictment of a people who will not fear Yahweh (5:20–31).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Lying prophets

The prophets speak falsely, the priests rule by their own authority, and the people approve. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Changes of speaker

Speakers change without announcement, and the people’s words are quoted inside Yahweh’s speech.

This verse begins a direct quotation from Yahweh, although the text does not say who is speaking. You may wish to indicate that Yahweh is the speaker in your translation, using a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

# Jeremiah 6 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Poetry throughout: alarm to flee the army from the north (6:1–8), Yahweh’s verdict on people who will not listen (6:9–21), terror as the army advances (6:22–26), and Jeremiah as a tester of metal (6:27–30).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Uncircumcised ear

In [6:10](../06/10.md), the covenant sign becomes an image for ears that will not hear Yahweh. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/circumcise]])

# Jeremiah 7 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh commands Jeremiah to preach at the gate of the temple, calling Judah to amend its conduct and warning that the sanctuary will not protect it.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Trust in the temple

The people assumed the [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/temple]] guaranteed their safety; Yahweh cites [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/shiloh]], a sanctuary he destroyed.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

# Jeremiah 8 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Yahweh’s judgment speech from chapter 7, moving from desecrated graves (verses 1–3), to the refusal to repent (verses 4–13), to invasion and lament (verses 14–22).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The host of the heavens

The people worshiped the sun, moon, and stars as gods. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/falsegod]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Unmarked speaker changes

The speaker shifts among Yahweh, the people, and the prophet without introduction, notably at verses 14, 18, and 19.

Jeremiah is using **the declaration of Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

The pronoun **they** refers to the enemies whom Yahweh will bring against Judah, whom he does not name here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Judah’s enemies will bring out the bones of the kings of Judah]

Yahweh is speaking as if the stars were a **host**, that is, an army drawn up in the sky. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to all of the many stars that fill the sky]

The pronoun **they** refers to the dead people whose bones will be spread out, not to the enemies who bring the bones out of the graves. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [which those dead people loved and which those dead people served]

Yahweh is speaking as if worshiping these heavenly bodies were traveling behind them, since he says that the people **walked after** them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and that they followed as their gods]

The expressions **They will not be gathered** and **they will not be buried** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [No one will gather them, and no one will bury them]

Yahweh is speaking as if the unburied bones were **dung**, something worthless that is left lying on the ground. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They will lie discarded and worthless on the surface of the ground]

This could mean: (1) Yahweh is telling Jeremiah what to say, so **I** refers to Jeremiah or (2) Yahweh is speaking about himself, so **I** refers to Yahweh. In either case, the pronoun **them** refers to the people of Judah and Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And I will say to the people of Judah and Jerusalem]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says this to you]

Yahweh is using the question form to appeal to what everyone knows, that people who fall down get up again. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Certainly those who fall down will get up again!]

Yahweh is using the question form to appeal to what everyone knows, that a person who wanders off the road turns around and comes back. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [If one turns away, then he certainly does return!]

# Jeremiah 9 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is mostly poetry, moving from Jeremiah’s lament over his people’s deceit to Yahweh’s sentence of refining, desolation, and exile. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lament]])

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Circumcision of the heart

Verses 25–26 contrast bodily circumcision with the inward loyalty to Yahweh that Israel lacks.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Changes of speaker

The speaker shifts between Jeremiah and Yahweh without introduction, and verses 15, 19, and 22 nest quotations within quotations.

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if his head were **waters** and as if his eyes were **a fountain of tears**. He means that he wants to weep continually for his people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I could produce tears without ceasing]

Jeremiah is referring to all of the time by naming two major components, **day** and **night**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [continually]

Jeremiah is using the adjective **slain** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [for the people who have been killed among]

Here Jeremiah is speaking of his fellow Israelites as if they were a **daughter**. He uses this expression to speak of his people tenderly, as a father would speak of his own child. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my people, whom I love as my own child]

Jeremiah is using **Who will give me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I wish that I had.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [If only I had a lodging place of travelers in the desert]

Here Jeremiah is speaking of his people as if they were **adulterers**. He means that they have been unfaithful to Yahweh. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For all of them are unfaithful to Yahweh]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people’s tongues were **their bow**, which they bend by treading on it in order to shoot lies. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they prepare their tongues as weapons]

Yahweh is using **from evil thing to evil thing they go** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they commit one wicked act after another.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For they proceed from one wicked act to another]

Jeremiah is using **the declaration of Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Yahweh is saying what he wants each person to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [Each one of you must beware of your neighbor]

Here the masculine term **brother** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [do not trust any brother or sister]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **deceives** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [every brother certainly deceives]

Here Yahweh is speaking of habitual behavior as if it were the way a person **walks**. He means that every neighbor regularly slanders others. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and every neighbor habitually slanders others]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by doing what is wicked]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if deceit were a place where a person could live, since he says that Jeremiah’s **dwelling** is **in the midst of deceit**. He means that the people all around Jeremiah are constantly deceitful. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You live among people who are constantly deceitful]
The pronoun **Your** refers to Jeremiah, whom Yahweh is addressing here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You, Jeremiah, dwell]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **deceit**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [among people who act deceitfully; because they are deceitful]

# Jeremiah 10 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter contrasts the worthless idols of the nations with Yahweh, the living God and creator (verses 1–16), then announces the coming exile and Jeremiah’s lament (verses 17–25).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Making idols

Verses 3–5, 9, and 14 describe craftsmen shaping [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/falsegod]] from wood and overlaying them with silver and gold.

### Jeremiah complains that evil men prosper

Jeremiah complains that evil men prosper. He questions Yahweh’s justice. Yahweh’s response: if Jeremiah is upset by the people of Anathoth, how will he face enemies in Jerusalem? (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/evil]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/justice]])

Yahweh gives a gracious offer to the Gentile nations. If the other nations who have been against Judah leave their idols and worship God, then God will allow them to return to their lands. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/grace]])

### Do not pray for the people

God told Jeremiah not to pray for the people because God was punishing them. This was meant to be an illustration for Jeremiah. Jeremiah was not to pray because the punishment was already determined. Yahweh is going to use the Gentile nations to punish Judah. This would have been very offensive to the Jews. They would have also been surprised to learn that Yahweh was using the Gentile nations to punish his people. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 16:19–21. This poem also continues in chapter 17, and these should be seen as one section.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Coming punishment

The punishment that is prophesied in this chapter will happen quickly. The author gives many illustrations which describe how quickly this punishment will come. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]])

### Israel restored

God will bring his people back from captivity. Even though the punishment of Judah will be great, Yahweh promised a future restoration. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promise]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/restore]])

Note: Here the word “cup” represents the drink that the cup holds. Alternate translation: [none must give a comforting drink]
Alternate translation: [a house where people are feasting]
Jeremiah often uses these words to introduce an important message from Yahweh. See how you translated this in [Jeremiah 6:6](../06/06.md).
Alternate translation: [Look] or [Listen] or [Pay attention to what I am about to tell you]

Here the word “your” is plural and refers to the people of Israel. The idiom means that Yahweh will do this where they can see. Alternate translation: [in front of you] or [where you can see] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])
This idiom means during their lifetime. Alternate translation: [during your lifetime]

Quote: the sound of joy and the sound of gladness, the sound of the groom and the sound of the bride
Note: See how you translated this in [Jeremiah 7:34](../07/34.md).

Quote: worshiped and bowed down to them
Note: The words “bowed down to” mean basically the same thing as “worshiped” and describe the posture that people used in worship. God said essentially the same thing twice for emphasis.
Alternate translation: [ancestors. Look at these people and you will see that each person]

Quote: walking by the stubbornness of his wicked heart
Note: Yahweh speaks of a person’s actions as if the person were walking along a path. Alternate translation: [stubbornly doing the wicked things that he wants to do] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])
Alternate translation: [who does what I tell him to do]
Yahweh speaks of forcefully removing the people from the land as if he were throwing them from the land. Alternate translation: [force you to leave this land and go]
The mention of both “day” and “night” means all the time. Alternate translation: [all the time] or [continually]
The word “behold” here alerts us to pay attention to the surprising information that follows.

Quote: when it will no longer be said
Note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [when people will no longer say]

“As surely as Yahweh is alive.” The people use this expression to show that what they say next is certainly true. This is a way of making a solemn promise. See how you translated this in [Jeremiah 4:2](../04/02.md). Alternate translation: [I solemnly swear]

Quote: I will send for many fishermen … so they will fish the people out
Note: Yahweh speaks of enemy armies who will attack and kill the people as if they were fishermen who are catching fish.

Quote: I will send for many hunters so they will hunt for them among
Note: Yahweh speaks of enemy armies who will attack and kill the people as if they were hunters who are hunting animals.

Quote: my eye is on all their ways
Note: Here the word “eye” represents Yahweh who sees all that they do. Alternate translation: [I am watching everything they do]

Quote: they cannot be hidden from before me
Note: Here the word “they” may refer either to the people or to their actions. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they cannot hide from me] or [they cannot hide their ways from me]

Quote: Their iniquity cannot be concealed from before my eyes
Note: Here the word “eyes” represents Yahweh who sees. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [They cannot conceal their iniquity from me] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

Quote: for their polluting of my land
Note: Yahweh speaks of causing the land to be unacceptable to him as if the people had polluted the land. Alternate translation: [because they have polluted my land]

Quote: for their filling my inheritance with their disgusting idols
Note: The idiom “to fill” means that they have placed many idols in the land. Alternate translation: [because they have filled my inheritance with their disgusting idols] or [because their disgusting idols are everywhere in my inheritance].
Yahweh speaks of the land as if it were his inheritance that he has claimed as a permanent possession. Alternate translation: [the land that is my inheritance]
Here Jeremiah begins speaking to Yahweh.

Quote: my stronghold and my refuge, my place of safety
Note: Jeremiah speaks of Yahweh as a place where enemies cannot attack him. He repeats the same idea three times.

Quote: The nations will go to you
Note: Here the word “nations” represents the people from the nations. Alternate translation: [The people from the nations will go to you]
This is an idiom that means the farthest places on the earth. Alternate translation: [the farthest places on the earth]
Here the word “deceit” refers to false gods. Alternate translation: [our ancestors inherited nothing but false gods]

Quote: They are empty; there is no profit in them
Note: Here the words “They” and “them” refer to the false gods that the ancestors taught them to believe in. The two phrases mean basically the same thing, with the second explaining how they “are empty.”

Quote: Do people make gods for themselves? But they are not gods
Note: The people ask this rhetorical question to emphasize that people cannot make gods for themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement. Alternate translation: [People cannot make gods for themselves. The things that they make are not gods]
“Therefore, indeed.” Here Yahweh begins speaking. The word “see” adds emphasis to what follows.

Quote: I will cause them to know
Note: Here the word “them” refers to the people from the nations. Yahweh repeats this phrase for emphasis.

Here the word “hand” refers to power and authority. The two phrases mean basically the same thing and emphasize Yahweh’s great power. Alternate translation: [my great power] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]])

Quote: they will know that Yahweh is my name
Note: Here the word “name” refers to Yahweh’s entire person. Alternate translation: [they will know that I am Yahweh, the true God]

# Jeremiah 17 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 17:1–18. This poem is a continuation of 16:19–21, and these should be seen as one section.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Trusting God or humans

Trust is an important part of this chapter. Those who trust in human wisdom will not prosper. Those who trust in God will have all of their needs met. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/trust]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/wise]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Simile

The person who depends on the power of other people is compared to a bush in the desert which always has to struggle for life. But the person who trusts in God is like a tree growing by a stream and has all his needs supplied. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

Quote: The sin of Judah is written … on the horns of your altars
Note: Yahweh speaks of Judah’s sins being so great that they cannot stop committing them as if someone had engraved their sin permanently.

Quote: The sin of Judah is written
Note: Here the word “Judah” represents the people of Judah. This may be expressed in active form. Alternate translation: [Someone has written the sin of Judah]
This may be expressed in active form. Alternate translation: [Someone has engraved it]

Quote: engraved on the tablet of their hearts
Note: The sinful habits of the people are spoken of as if their sins had been engraved on their own hearts. The word “hearts” refers to the whole person: their thoughts, emotions, and actions. Alternate translation: [engraved in their very beings]

Quote: on the horns of your altars
Note: The word “horns” refers to the projections on the corners of the altars.

Quote: your wealth and all your treasures
Note: The words “wealth” and “treasures” mean the same thing and refer to anything that they consider valuable.
This refers to things that people steal or take by force.

Quote: You will lose the inheritance that I gave to you
Note: Yahweh speaks of the land as if it were an inheritance that he had given to the people of Judah as a permanent possession. Alternate translation: [You will lose the land that I have given to you as an inheritance]

Quote: you have ignited a fire in my wrath, which will burn forever
Note: Yahweh speaks of the fierceness of his anger as if his anger were a fire that burns those with whom he is angry. Alternate translation: [you have made me so angry that my anger will be like a fire that will burn forever]

Quote: The person who trusts in mankind is accursed
Note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will curse any person who trusts in mankind]
Here the word “flesh” represents humans. Alternate translation: [he depends on mere humans for strength]

Quote: turns his heart away from Yahweh
Note: Here the word “heart” refers to the thoughts and emotions. Alternate translation: [turns his devotion away from Yahweh]
The person who trusts in man instead of Yahweh will be like a plant that struggles to survive in an infertile land.

Quote: the wilderness, barren land without inhabitants
Note: The phrase “barren land without inhabitants” describes and means basically the same thing as “wilderness.” Alternate translation: [the barren wilderness where no person lives]

Quote: he will be like a tree planted by water
Note: The person who trusts in Yahweh will always prosper, just like a tree does when it is planted by a river. It is not affected when there is no rain. Alternate translation: [he will be like a tree that someone has planted by water]

Quote: It will not fear the heat when it comes … It is not anxious in a year of drought
Note: Yahweh speaks of a tree that draws its water from a stream being unaffected by heat and drought as if the tree were unafraid of these things. Alternate translation: [The heat will not affect it when it comes … No harm is caused to it in a year of drought]
Here the word “heart” refers to the minds and thoughts of people. Alternate translation: [The human mind is more deceitful]

The speaker uses this rhetorical question to emphasize that no one can understand the human heart. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement. Alternate translation: [no one can understand it.]
Here the word “hearts” represents the emotions. Alternate translation: [who tests the emotions]
Here a person’s behavior is spoken of as if it were the paths along which he walks. Alternate translation: [according to how he lives]
Here the results of a person’s actions are spoken of as if they were fruit. Alternate translation: [what he has done]

Quote: A partridge hatches an egg … become rich unjustly
Note: This analogy of a bird that hatches another bird’s eggs is meant to illustrate a rich man who makes his money by robbing others.

Quote: when half his days are over
Note: Here the word “days” stands for someone’s entire life. Alternate translation: [when he has lived only half of his life]
The riches are spoken of as if they were servants who would abandon their owner. Alternate translation: [he will lose his wealth]
Alternate translation: [at the end of his life]

Quote: The place of our temple is a glorious throne
Note: Jeremiah speaks of the temple being a “glorious throne” because it is there that Yahweh dwells and rules.
This refers to Mount Zion in Jerusalem.
Here the word “you” refers to Yahweh.

Quote: those in the land who turn away from you will be written in the earth
Note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [you will write in the dust those in the land who turn away from you]

Quote: will be written in the earth
Note: This could mean: (1) this is a metaphor in which Yahweh speaks of people dying and being forgotten as if someone writes their names in the dust, and those names quickly disappear. Alternate translation: [will disappear like names that someone writes in the dust] or (2) the word “earth” is a metonym for the place of the dead. The phrase is a metaphor in which Yahweh speaks of people going to the place of the dead as if someone enrolled their names in the records of those who have died. Alternate translation: [will join those in the place of the dead]

Quote: Yahweh, the fountain of living waters
Note: Jeremiah speaks of Yahweh being the source of life as if he were a fountain of living waters. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, who is like a fountain of living waters]
Jeremiah speaks of fresh, running water as if it were living water. Alternate translation: [the fountain of fresh, running water]

Quote: I will be healed … I will be rescued
Note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [you really will have healed me … you really will have rescued me]

Quote: For you are my song of praise
Note: This could mean: (1) “For you are the one whom I praise” or (2) “For you are the reason I sing praise.”
Alternate translation: [Look] or [Listen] or [Pay attention to what I am about to tell you.]
Here the word “me” refers to Jeremiah and the word “they” to his enemies.

Quote: Where is the word of Yahweh?
Note: The people use this question to ridicule Jeremiah because the things that he said had not yet happened. It can also be translated as a statement. Alternate translation: [Where are the things that Yahweh told you would happen?] or [The things that Yahweh told you would happen have not happened.] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])
Alternate translation: [Let what Yahweh has said happen]

Quote: I did not run from being a shepherd following you
Note: Jeremiah speaks of leading and caring for the people as if he were a shepherd caring for sheep. He speaks of his abandoning that work as if he were running away from it.
Alternate translation: [I did not desire]

Quote: the proclamations that came from my lips
Note: Here the word “lips” represents Jeremiah who spoke. Alternate translation: [the proclamations that I spoke]
If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I made them]
Jeremiah speaks of Yahweh as a place where enemies cannot attack him.
Alternate translation: [in times of calamity]

Quote: May my pursuers be ashamed, but do not let me be ashamed
Note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Bring shame on my pursuers, but do not bring shame on me]

Quote: May they be dismayed, but do not let me be dismayed
Note: This phrase means basically the same thing as the previous one and adds emphasis to Jeremiah’s prayer. Alternate translation: [Make them very afraid, but do not make me afraid]

Quote: shatter them with a double share of destruction
Note: Jeremiah speaks of Yahweh destroying his enemies as if they were objects that Yahweh would shatter. The idiom “a double share” means to give twice as much. Alternate translation: [shatter them with complete destruction] or [destroy them twice as much] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

Quote: then in all the other gates of Jerusalem
Note: The verb may be supplied from the previous phrase. Alternate translation: [then go and stand in all the other gates of Jerusalem]

Quote: for the sake of your lives
Note: Alternate translation: [to protect your lives]

Quote: They did not listen or pay attention
Note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing and emphasize that the people refused to listen. Alternate translation: [They refused to listen] or [They refused to obey]
Jeremiah speaks of the people being stubborn as if they had made their necks stiff and unmovable. Alternate translation: [became stubborn]

Quote: those who sit on David’s throne
Note: Here the throne that the king of Judah sits on is represented as “David’s throne.” See how you translated this in [Jeremiah 13:13](../13/13.md). Alternate translation: [those who sit on Judah’s throne] or [the kings of the nation of Judah]

Quote: this city will be inhabited forever
Note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people will inhabit this city forever]

Quote: I will light a fire in its gates
Note: Alternate translation: [I will set the gates of Jerusalem on fire]
If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people cannot put it out]

# Jeremiah 18 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 18:13–17, 19–23.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Attacking Jeremiah

Things were so bad in Judah, they even attacked Jeremiah. To attack Yahweh’s prophet was to attack Yahweh himself. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Simile

Like a potter can change what he is making from one type of pot to another, God can change his plans and not punish people if they repent. The image of God as a potter and mankind as clay is an important one in Scripture. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/repent]] and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])
“the workshop of the potter.” A potter is someone who makes pots from clay.
The word “behold” alerts us to a new person in the story. Your language may have a way of doing this.
The potter’s wheel is a small table that spins. A potter uses it to make pots.

Quote: the pot he was making from the clay was spoiled in the potter’s hand
Note: The word “spoiled” means that something about the pot made the potter unhappy. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the pot that the potter was making with his hands was not good]
Alternate translation: [was forming] or [was shaping]

Quote: he returned the clay and formed it into another pot
Note: He stopped making the pot, crushed the clay back into a lump, and then used that lump of clay to make another pot.

Quote: that was pleasing in his eyes
Note: Here the word “eyes” represents sight and sight represents one’s opinion. Alternate translation: [that he thought was good]

Quote: Should I not be able to act like this potter with you, house of Israel?
Note: With this question, Yahweh emphasizes his authority to do as he pleases with Israel. Alternate translation: [I am allowed to act toward you, house of Israel, like the potter acts toward the clay.]

The word “house” is a metonym for the family that lives in the house. In this case it refers to the kingdom of Israel. See how you translated this in [Jeremiah 3:18](../03/18.md). Alternate translation: [Israel] or [kingdom of Israel] or [people of Israel]
Alternate translation: [Pay attention, because what I am about to say is both true and important]

Quote: Like clay in a potter’s hand—that is how you are in my hand
Note: Yahweh compares his being able to remake Israel as he see fit to the way that the potter is able to remake a lump of clay as he sees fit.

Quote: tear it down, or destroy it
Note: These two expressions basically mean the same thing.
Alternate translation: [withhold] or [not bring]

Quote: build it up or plant it
Note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing.

Quote: if it does evil in my eyes
Note: Here the word “it” refers to a nation or kingdom, which is a metonym for the people in that nation or kingdom. The word “eyes” represents seeing, and seeing represents thoughts or judgment. Alternate translation: [if the people of that nation do things that I consider to be evil] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

Here the word “voice” represents the words that Yahweh speaks. Here, “not listening” is an idiom that means that they do not obey. Alternate translation: [not obeying what I say] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])
This tells the reader to pay special attention to what follows. Alternate translation: [Look] or [Listen] or [Pay attention to what I am about to tell you]

Quote: I am about to form disaster against you. I am about to devise a plan against you
Note: Yahweh speaks of planning disaster as if disaster were an object that he forms, like the potter would form clay. The second sentence repeats the same idea as the first using different words. Alternate translation: [I am about to devise a plan to bring disaster against you] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])
Alternate translation: [make a plan]
Yahweh speaks of a person’s lifestyle as if it were a “way” or path along which the person walks. Alternate translation: [his wicked way of living]

Quote: so your ways and your practices will bring good to you
Note: The words “ways” and “practices” both refer to a person’s actions and general lifestyle. Alternate translation: [so your actions will result in good happening to you]
The word “they” refers to the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem.

Here, this idiom could mean: (1) the people do not care about what Jeremiah will say to them. Alternate translation: [We do not care what you say] or (2) The people do not think that anything good will come of what Jeremiah tells them to do. Alternate translation: [What you are saying will not work]

Quote: what his evil, stubborn heart desires
Note: Here the word “heart” represents the person’s mind or will. Alternate translation: [what his evil, stubborn mind desires] or [whatever evil things that we stubbornly want to do]

Quote: Ask the nations, who has ever heard of such a thing as this?
Note: Here the word “nations” represents the people in the nations. Yahweh asks this question to scold the people of Judah. Alternate translation: [Ask the nations if any of them have ever heard of such a thing as this.] or [Nowhere on earth has anyone ever heard of such a thing like this.]

Quote: The virgin Israel has committed a horrible act
Note: It was common to refer to nations as if they were women. Yahweh speaks of Israel being pure and faithful towards him as if she were a virgin and of Israel being unfaithful to him as if she had “committed a horrible act.” Alternate translation: [Israel, who is like a virgin, has done something horrible] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

Quote: Does the snow in Lebanon ever leave the rocky hills on its sides?
Note: Yahweh asks this rhetorical question to emphasize that the snow on the mountains never melts. Alternate translation: [The snow in Lebanon never leaves the rocky hills on its sides.]

Quote: the rocky hills on its sides
Note: Alternate translation: [the sides of the rocky hills]

Quote: Are the mountain streams coming from far away ever destroyed, those cold streams?
Note: Yahweh asks this rhetorical question to emphasize that the mountain streams never cease to flow. He speaks of the streams drying up as if they were destroyed. Alternate translation: [Those cold mountain streams that come from far away never cease to flow.] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

Quote: been made to stumble in their paths
Note: Yahweh speaks of a person’s lifestyle as if it were a path along which he walks, and of living unfaithfully to him as if the person stumbled along the path. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [this caused them to stumble in their paths] or [it is like they stumbled while walking on a path] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

Quote: they have left the ancient paths to walk lesser paths
Note: Yahweh speaks of a person’s lifestyle as if it were a path along which he walks. Here, “the ancient paths” represents the way that Yahweh had told their ancestors to live and “lesser paths” represents living unfaithfully to Yahweh.
The word “horror” may be translated with a verbal phrase. Alternate translation: [will become something that horrifies people]
The word “hissing” refers to a sound that shows strong disapproval and can be translated with a verbal phrase. Alternate translation: [an object at which people will always hiss]
Here the word “her” refers to “Their land.”

Quote: I will scatter them before their enemies like an eastern wind
Note: Yahweh speaks of causing the people to flee before their enemies as if he were an eastern wind that scatters dust and debris. Alternate translation: [I will be like an eastern wind and scatter them before their enemies] or [I will scatter them before their enemies like an eastern wind scatters dust and debris]
Here the word “them” refers to “my people.”

Quote: I will show them my back, and not my face
Note: “I will turn my back toward them, and not my face.” Turning one’s back towards someone is a symbolic action that represents rejection and turning one’s face towards someone is a symbolic action that represents favor. Alternate translation: [I will reject them and not act favorably towards them]

Quote: let us make plots against Jeremiah
Note: Alternate translation: [let us make plans to harm Jeremiah]

Quote: the law will never perish from the priests, or advice from the wise men, or words from the prophets
Note: The words “will never perish” can be supplied to each of these phrases. This can also be expressed in positive terms. Alternate translation: [the law will never perish from the priests, and advice will never perish from the wise men, and words will never perish from the prophets] or [the priests will always have the law, the wise men will always give advice, and the prophets will always speak]
Here “words” represents messages that the prophets speak from Yahweh. Alternate translation: [words of Yahweh from the prophets]
The people speak of speaking harmful words against Jeremiah as if their words were weapons with which they attack him. Alternate translation: [say things that will harm him]
Here Jeremiah begins speaking to Yahweh.

Quote: Will disaster from them really be my reward for being good to them?
Note: Jeremiah asks this question to emphasize that good actions should not be repaid with bad things. Alternate translation: [Disaster from them should not be my reward for being good to them.]

Quote: they have dug a pit for me
Note: Jeremiah speaks of his enemies planning to kill him as if they had dug a pit in which to trap him.

Quote: to cause your fury to turn away from them
Note: Here the word “fury” represents the punishment that Yahweh intended to inflict upon them.

Quote: give their children over to famine
Note: The idiom “give over” means to place a person in the power of another person. Jeremiah speaks of “famine” as if it were a person who could have power over others. Alternate translation: [cause their children to die from famine] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

Quote: give them to the hands of those who use the sword
Note: Here the word “hands” represents power. Alternate translation: [cause those who use the sword to have power over them] or [cause them to die in battle]

Quote: let their women become bereaved and widows
Note: “let the children and husbands of their women die.” The word “bereaved” refers to a woman whose children have all died.
The verb may be supplied from the previous phrase.

Quote: their young men killed by the sword in battle
Note: The verb may be supplied from the previous phrase. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [let people kill their young men with swords in battle] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

Quote: Let a distressed shout be heard
Note: The phrase “a distressed shout” can be translated with a verbal phrase. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Let people hear a distressed shout] or [Let people hear others shout in distress]

Quote: For they have dug a pit to capture me and have hidden traps for my feet
Note: These two phrases share similar meanings. Jeremiah speaks of his enemies planning to kill him as if they had dug a pit for him to fall into and set traps in which to capture him. (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])
See how you translated this in [Jeremiah 18:20](../18/20.md).

Quote: have hidden traps for my feet
Note: Here the word “feet” represents Jeremiah. Alternate translation: [have hidden traps for me] or [have hidden traps for me to step on]

Quote: Do not wipe their sins away from you
Note: Jeremiah speaks of Yahweh forgiving his enemies’ sins as if someone had written their sins down and Yahweh would erase them. This phrase means the same thing as the previous phrase. Alternate translation: [Do not pardon their sins]

Quote: let them be overthrown before you
Note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [let people overthrow them in your presence]

Quote: in the time of your wrath
Note: The word “wrath” can be translated with a verb. Alternate translation: [when you are still angry with them]

# Jeremiah 19 General Notes

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### People horrified

The destruction of Jerusalem will be so complete that it will leave dead bodies everywhere and horrify people who see it.
This is the name of a valley south of the city of Jerusalem, where people sacrificed to false gods. See how you translated this in [Jeremiah 7:31](../07/31.md).
Jeremiah often uses these words to introduce an important message from Yahweh. See how you translated this in [Jeremiah 6:6](../06/06.md).
Alternate translation: [Look] or [Listen] or [Pay attention to what I am about to tell you]

Quote: the ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle
Note: Here “ears … will tingle” is an idiom that means everyone will be shocked by what they hear. Alternate translation: [it will shock everyone who hears of it]
This could mean: (1) “will ring” or (2) “will quiver.”
Here the word “they” refers to the people of Judah.

Quote: filled this place with innocent blood
Note: Here “innocent blood” represents the murder of innocent people. Alternate translation: [murdered many innocent people in this place]

Quote: nor did it enter my mind

### Pashhur

This chapter prophesied punishment against a specific leader named Pashhur. He was in charge of protecting the temple and had Jeremiah beaten and arrested. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/temple]])

In Hebrew, the word for “message” can also mean “burden.” In translations that are using footnotes, you may want to explain the wordplay in a footnote. In translations that are not using footnotes or which will primarily be distributed in an oral form, you may need a sentence like “What message has the Lord burdened you with now?” or “You (plural) call God’s message a heavy burden on you.”

# Jeremiah 25 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 25:30–38.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Seventy years

Babylon will rule over Judah for seventy years. Because Yahweh is just, he will soon punish Babylon for their evil actions. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/justice]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/evil]])

# Jeremiah 31 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 31:1–6, 8–22, 35–37.

The ULT sets [31:29](../31/29.md) farther to the right on the page than the rest of the text because it is an important quotation.

This chapter begins with a transition from the previous chapter. “At that time” is a reference to the day of restoration mentioned in [Jeremiah 30:24](../30/24.md). (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/restore]])

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The new covenant

This chapter is an important teaching regarding the new covenant. God will make a new covenant that will bring forgiveness of sins and a desire to obey God. Scholars disagree about whether this new covenant has begun. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenant]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/forgive]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]])

# Jeremiah 34 General Notes

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Law of Moses

According to the law of Moses, the people were required to free their indebted slaves after a period of time. The king led them in freeing their fellow Israelites whom they held as slaves, but later they changed their minds and enslaved them again. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lawofmoses]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Actions with cultural meaning

When the people of Israel made a sacred promise to God, they cut a calf in two and passed between its parts. It was a very serious sin not to do what one had promised. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promise]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]] and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

After Jeremiah prophesied the destruction of Judah, the people did not believe him. Judah was conquered and destroyed. # Jeremiah 49 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

The ULT sets the lines in 49:1–11, 14–27, 29–33, 37–39 farther to the right on the page than the rest of the text because they are part of a long quotation.

Jeremiah’s prophesies about other nations conclude in this chapter. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]])

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Covenant with Abraham

Ammon is destroyed because it drove the people of the tribe of Gad from their homeland. This is in line with the promises of the covenant Yahweh made with Abraham to curse those who curse Abraham’s descendants. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promise]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenant]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/curse]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Rhetorical questions

There are many rhetorical questions in this chapter. The purpose of these rhetorical questions is to convict those Yahweh addresses. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])
Jeremiah often uses these words to introduce an important message from Yahweh. See how you translated a similar phrase in [Jeremiah 6:6](../06/06.md).

# Jeremiah 50 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 50:1–5, 6–46.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Babylon destroyed

Babylon will be conquered and the Jews will return to their homeland. At this time, Babylon controlled almost the entire Near East. The fulfillment of this prophecy would have been unthinkable. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/fulfill]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

The author sometimes uses the term “Israel” to refer to the people of the old northern kingdom of Israel, and at other times to the nation of Israel as a whole. He switches between these uses several times without warning the reader. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])
